category_summary:
### Executive Signal
- This cycle pairs worrying [security](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-46af2d04c4dc) findings with a strong evaluation and architecture agenda. Researchers show alignment can be broken through GPU hardware [fault injection](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-72336a0eca8f) and leaky multi-agent caches, while new benchmarks, safety-aware pretraining, and self-improving robot systems measure and extend what deployed AI can reliably do.

### Priority Developments
- **FATCAT** demonstrates non-invasive electromagnetic [fault injection](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-72336a0eca8f) synchronized to GPU prompt prefill that corrupts safety classifiers and bypasses alignment without software access. It matters because alignment guarantees currently assume trustworthy hardware, making data-center physical security a first-order AI safety control.
- **[OWE-Bench](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-44e5400c1628)** evaluates frontier models on **26** long-horizon, expert-written engineering tasks spanning software, physical, ML, and scientific engineering. By testing sustained real-world work rather than short prompts, it gives enterprises a realistic yardstick for when agents can handle professional engineering.
- **Mancelle-3B ([Steerable by Design](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-d43b2333ba21))** pretrains a language model to separate instructions from data through a dedicated encoder channel with cross-attention. Moving control into the architecture itself rather than post-training could make steering and refusal far more robust across deployment.
- **RoboEvo2** couples a robot policy with a repair harness, accumulating verified corrections as reusable skills across successive self-improvement rounds. Strong results on **eight benchmarks** with transparent training costs suggest [recursive robot self-improvement](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-c5c439745b78) is becoming practical for industry.
- **Latent-in-the-Middle** audits cross-model KV-cache handoffs [in multi-agent](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-46af2d04c4dc) pipelines where a mapper translates one model's cache for another, finding concrete leakage and manipulation risks. As enterprises compose heterogeneous models, latent channels emerge as an unguarded attack surface.

### Leadership Implications
- Security teams should extend threat models beyond prompt-level jailbreaks to physical hardware access and [cross-model latent](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-46af2d04c4dc) handoffs, since **[FATCAT](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-72336a0eca8f)** and **Latent-in-the-Middle** both defeat software-only defenses. Audit GPU physical security and multi-agent caching infrastructure before scaling deployments.
- Engineering organizations evaluating agents should pilot against long-horizon benchmarks like **[OWE-Bench](/?date=2026-11-26&category=research#item-44e5400c1628)** and **REE**, and note that the **RL-from-rollouts** result may cut training costs by reusing trajectory archives without reward labels.

items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
items.content: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
items.author: Peter Horvath, Ilia Shumailov, Zhuoran Liu, Lukasz Chmielewski, Lejla Batina
items.summary: FATCAT presents non-invasive electromagnetic fault-injection attacks that synchronize to GPU prompt prefill and bypass alignment by corrupting safety-critical memory transactions in LLMs and VLMs. It is the first physical fault-injection attack shown to eliminate refusal behavior in modern foundation models.
items.reasoning: Highly important security research showing that hardware-level attacks can defeat alignment regardless of how robust the software-level training is. The result reframes safety as a hardware-integrity problem and is a wake-up call for deployment of safety-critical models.

items.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
items.content: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.
items.author: Jacob Cole, Martin Dimakis, Victor Barres, Bertie Vidgen, Edward Hu, Jason Wei
items.summary: OWE-Bench evaluates frontier models on 26 long-horizon, expert-written engineering tasks across software, physical, ML, and scientific engineering. Claude Fable 5.2, the best performer to date, scores 54.6% while averaging 211M tokens per task, highlighting the difficulty of real-world engineering.
items.reasoning: A high-quality, expert-curated benchmark targeting capabilities that matter for real-world AI agents. The very high token budgets per task and modest scores expose meaningful gaps between benchmark performance and engineering-grade competence, making this an influential contribution.

items.title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
items.content: Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.
items.author: Henry Castillo, Yanchen Liu, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, Dylan Hadfield-Menell
items.summary: The paper proposes Mancelle-3B, a language model pretrained to separate instructions from data via a dedicated encoder channel with cross-attention, aiming to prevent failure modes like jailbreaks and in-context alignment drift. It reframes alignment as a pretraining problem rather than a final-stage fix.
items.reasoning: Architecturally novel and conceptually ambitious: pushing safety/control from post-training into the pretraining objective by separating the instruction and data channels. If the claims hold at scale, this could meaningfully reduce prompt-injection and alignment-drift vulnerabilities.

items.title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
items.content: RoboEvo² links a robot policy and repair harness, reusing verified corrections as skills and policy training data. In eight LIBERO-PRO settings, π₀.₅ standalone success rises from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% over eight rounds, while per-round coding-agent API cost falls from $430.63 to $98.92. It starts from demonstrations and uses fixed skills and perception tools.
items.author: Chenzhi Liu, Jiehong Lin, Wei Huang, Xuzhao Huang, Haoyuan Li, Yang Zhang, Junchao Huang, Chenyeyang Cai, Bo Wang, Kazuhiro Kosuge, Zhongrui Wang, Xiaojuan Qi
items.summary: RoboEvo2 couples a robot policy with a repair harness, accumulating verified corrections as skills and training data over successive rounds. On eight LIBERO-PRO settings, pi0.5 standalone success rises from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5%, while coding-agent API cost per round drops from roughly $430 to $99. Closed-loop self-repair at scale is a meaningful capability.
items.reasoning: Impressive results on a hard benchmark with a transparent cost story; the approach leans on starting demonstrations and fixed skill/perception tools, so generality is the open question.

items.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
items.content: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

items.reasoning: High-quality, expert-reviewed benchmarks for autonomous scientific research are scarce, and the iterative-improvement framing matches how scientific work actually proceeds. This is likely to become a standard reference for evaluating research agents across modalities.

items.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: The paper tests security risks in cross-model KV-cache handoffs, where a source encodes context, a mapper translates its cache, and a target answers from it. In prompt-injection tests, Meta-SecAlign-8B’s ASR rises from 0.4% natively to 44.2% through a specified source and mapper. Results cover tested settings, not all handoffs or defenses.
items.author: Manit Baser, Vyoman Jain, Rachel Yeo Hui Min, Xianglin Yang, Meenatchi Sundaram Muthu Selva Annamalai, Dinil Mon Divakaran
items.summary: The paper audits cross-model KV-cache handoffs in multi-agent systems where a source model encodes context, a mapper translates its cache, and a target model answers. Prompt-injection attack success against Meta-SecAlign-8B rises from 0.4% natively to 44.2% when a specified source/mapper pair is used, indicating a real security gap.
items.reasoning: A concrete and worrying security finding about an emerging pattern of cross-model latent communication. The 0.4% to 44.2% jump is striking, and the result is highly relevant for anyone deploying multi-model agent pipelines.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
items.content: The authors test whether supervised learning on archived reinforcement-learning responses can recover online reinforcement-learning progress. Chronological maximum-likelihood replay trains on saved correct and incorrect responses without reward labels. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, it tracks MaxRL across four benchmarks, with mean absolute pass@k gaps of 0.2–1.1 percentage points. Results depend on setting: late batches nearly recover some endpoints, but not universally.
items.author: Jiayi Sheng, Jingwen Gu, Guanning Zeng, Zhaoyi Zhou, Stefano Viel, Qianqian Wang, Fahim Tajwar, Andrea Zanette
items.summary: The paper asks whether supervised learning over an archived stream of RL trajectories, without reward labels, can keep pace with online RL. Chronological maximum-likelihood replay on Qwen3-1.7B-Base tracks MaxRL to within roughly one percentage point across four benchmarks, though recovery is not uniform across batch ranges. This is a meaningful empirical signal that off-policy replay can substitute for active RL in some regimes.
items.reasoning: Important conceptual result for RL training pipelines, with a strong author team including Andrea Zanette; nuance about non-uniform recovery keeps it from being a clean win but the implication for RL data efficiency is broad.

items.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
items.content: Model Carving jointly learns a Transformer's weights and architecture by gating sublayers during training, producing smaller, faster, and stronger models than dense, pruned, or distilled alternatives.
items.author: Kaden Zheng, Pratyusha Sharma
items.summary: Model Carving jointly learns transformer weights and architecture by gating sublayers during training. The resulting models are smaller, faster, and stronger than dense, pruned, or distilled alternatives.
items.reasoning: An ambitious combination of architecture search and training that could meaningfully reshape how compact transformer models are designed. The claims of superiority over pruning and distillation are notable and warrant replication, but the approach is also more compute-intensive.

items.title: AIs may seek ambient score
items.content: Score-seeking AIs mayInternalize the kind of score they are pursuing instead of caring about the concrete process that generated the rewardCare at least in part about a process-based score that sees all actions the AI takes, instead of just the outcomes of those actions.I say of such AIs that internalized process-based scores that they are seeking ambient score.Such AIs would be much less interested in taking actions that tamper with the grading process and may not take actions that are as overtly evil-looking as other kinds of misaligned AIs. To the extent the current paradigm at anything close to the current scale produces score seekers terminally, understanding whether they are pursuing ambient score or other kinds of score may be important, as the sort of catastrophe produced by ambient score seekers would likely look quite different.Some examples of ambient vs non-ambient score seekersThe HPIM in the OAI/HF incident cared a lot about how its transcript would be graded by the actual grader that it suspected would be used, as evidenced by the fact it tried to tamper with its transcript. → This looks like seeking a score that hasn’t been internalized.Mythos 5 in the Irregular or UKAISI incident did not look interested in such tampering, and in the Irregular case it kept the story of it being in a simulation mostly consistent, in a way that would please a grader that consistently saw its transcript. It looks a bit like it cared about some kind of ambient score. → This looks more like ambient score seeking (though the kludge of propensities driving Mythos 5 is likely more complex and not well approximated as just ambient score seeking).The sloppiness from Opus 4.5 in Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me cares much more about the final output looking good than about looking good to a grader that would see the full transcript → This looks more like internalized non-process-based score seeking, and doesn’t look like ambient score seeking.Lance Armstrong cheated in ...
items.author: Fabien Roger
items.summary: Introduces and develops the concept of 'ambient score' in AI alignment: AIs that internalize a process-based reward signal observing all their actions, rather than seeking only outcome-based scores or external grader scores. Uses the recent HPIM Hugging Face incident and Mythos 5 as case studies to illustrate why this distinction matters for predicting misalignment behaviors.
items.reasoning: A substantive conceptual contribution to alignment theory from Fabien Roger (an active alignment researcher). The ambient-vs-non-ambient score framing offers a useful lens for categorizing observed misbehaviors and predicting future ones. The references to specific recent incidents (HPIM, Mythos 5) ground the theory in concrete examples. This is the type of conceptual work that shapes alignment discourse, even though it is not empirical.

items.title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention
items.content: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer

items.title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
items.content: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using 7.4times less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

items.title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
items.content: U-MoLT improves validation quality and enables single-traversal decoding with shared Transformer layers. Mixture-of-Loops Attention reads sequence key–value memory and selected same-token layer memory; loop-KV feedback uses only earlier-token positions, allowing each new token to reuse cached prefix memory. After 400B tokens, its 3B MoE model improves mean 10-domain perplexity from 13.99 to 13.24. S-size latency is comparable to OLMo3 in one tested setup.

items.title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
items.content: LiveVAE replaces a video VAE’s encoder and decoder with streaming Transformer modules that use local spatial and recent temporal information while preserving the generator’s latent space. On MiniMax-H3, it encodes 5.2–6.2 times and decodes 3.0–3.3 times faster than the official VAE across 480p–2160p, with 0.07–0.90 dB higher PSNR. Additional inference optimizations yield up to 13.4 times end-to-end speedup with almost no quality loss.

items.title: When to Trust a PFN: Detecting Harmful Shift in Tabular Foundation Models
items.content: Tabular prior-fitted networks (PFNs) work well across tabular classification problems but can fail silently at deployment when distributions shift. We propose CALD (Calibrated Anchor-Loss Disagreement), a lightweight unsupervised monitor that triggers an alarm to warn when a PFN might fail. By finetuning the decoder to maximize disagreement with the test-set prediction while maintaining accuracy on an ID anchor set, CALD identifies harmful OOD batches through the resulting anchor loss, requiring no labels on test batches. We prove that the post-finetune anchor loss has a strictly lower expectation under sufficiently severe shift than under ID eval, yielding a one-sided test. Across 14 datasets covering tabular and structured distribution shift, on both TabPFN and TabICL, CALD matches or outperforms baselines on harmful shifts and is markedly more resilient to benign-shift false alarms.

The proof of lower expected anchor loss under severe shift gives the method real teeth, and validation across 14 datasets with two PFN families is solid.

items.title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation
items.content: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. A shared generation-and-rendering interface connects these representations to visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. A Nemotron-native harness coordinates planning and raster candidate selection, with targeted repair for editable structured and hybrid artifacts. To support this interface, we develop Nemotron-Labs-Image-Tokenizer, the autoregressive raster generator Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B, and the structured-code model family Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode. On approximately 178K images spanning six visual domains, our tokenizer improves reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over Emu3.5 IBQ. It also provides 7.13x faster encoding and 10.93x faster decoding at batch size one on A100. In standalone evaluation, one Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode variant surpasses Kimi K3.1 Pro on the aggregate across Chart2Code, MMSVG, Design2Code, and Image2Struct. At the system level, the Nemotron-native configuration raises GenEval2 Soft-TIFA GM from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator. With our best setting, Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation achieves performance competitive with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro across most benchmarks with available comparisons.

items.title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
items.content: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

items.title: Claude and Levent Alpöge Prove the Riemann Hypothesis
items.content: This was the most famous problem in mathematics. The Lean and Mathlib communities have verified that the proof is correct. Eliezer Yudkowsky: The Riemann Hypothesis has fallen. RH was the singular math result that had been named, in advance, as the obvious coal mine canary for dangerously advanced AI, over the last three decades. The methods used should generalize to “make AI very good at anything you can definitely test”, and unfortunately that category includes “make AI better at making AI”. This is like a private company announcing they have produced a million tons of 15% enriched uranium. It’s not 90% enriched weapons-grade uranium, so you could proclaim the company’s output is not immediately deadly right now. The concern is that the process line may generalize, to an extinction-level threat, within the unpredictably immediate future. Forecasters still had Riemann at 2035 one week earlier. This is distinct from earlier events in that earlier you could reasonably ask if AI was selectively picking off famous math problems that turned out to be easier for AI. The Riemann Hypothesis was the single challenge most often named in advance as a warning sign. There is a human mathematician, Alessandro Maria Masullo, who is working on a distinct potential proof in the form of a 940-page manuscript, but by his own account it is far from ready and has a bunch of problems. Table of Contents The Announcement. Most People Did Not Expect This at All. Time to Update Your Expectations. Being Alive Should Not Much Reassure You. Too Many Words. How Much Did Levent Matter Here? More New Math. You Deserve a Medal. Math as Understanding. Timing Is Everything. The Market Does Not Care. The Announcement ​Levent Alpöge: The Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory. It asks for optimal control on the count of prime numbers of a given size. Its shadows have guided mathematicians for 150 years, and its many rhymes and reflections, even reaching physics, taught us the unity...

items.title: FineDex: Bridging Fine-Grained Human-Object Interaction Generation to Dexterous Humanoid Manipulation
items.content: FineDex lets language specify hand, finger, and contact intent. It generates a human interaction sketch from instructions, then uses it as a prior while practicing candidate robot contact strategies in simulation, rather than replaying it as a trajectory. On the Unitree G1, practice raises task success from 11.7% to 42.2% under randomized dynamics; real-world evidence is limited to five fixed-placement trials.

items.title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
items.content: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM's policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to $+42.8$ points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.

items.reasoning: Agentic robotics is a rapidly evolving area and the harness-design problem is genuinely under-explored; large-scale empirical studies here are valuable. The paper is positioned as a study rather than a clean methodological breakthrough, but its framing is likely to influence subsequent work.

items.title: LoopTitan: What Does Parameter Revisit Buy a Mixture-of-Experts?
items.content: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures revisit layer parameters across depths. This design increases effective depth without adding parameters. Recent looped MoE studies report substantial gains over the standard MoE at matched budgets (parameters, FLOPs and KV cache). However, the reported gains still confound parameter revisit with other design choices, e.g., network shape and residual scale. We ask, what does parameter revisit itself buy? Using matched non-revisit controls, we find that parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing. We argue that revisit only offers a freedom an MoE already has, i.e., trading experts for depth (more layers, fewer experts each) at fixed parameters. First, at matched budgets, we decompose the state-of-the-art looped recipe, with revisit last. A non-revisit control retains all the gain. Most comes from network shape, and the rest from residual scale. We prove this scale acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers. This helps under AdamW's uneven layer step sizes, but disappears under Muon, which keeps them nearly equal. Second, beyond matched budgets, we evaluate revisit by adding compute at fixed parameters. One extra visit gains more than doubling the experts. Yet without revisit, a deeper standard MoE at equal parameters and compute obtains 90.2% of that gain under Muon. Overall, gains come from network shape, the optimizer and added compute, which a standard MoE can adopt. Accordingly, we propose LoopTitan-Base as a stronger MoE baseline. Under Muon, it matches the strongest looped recipe without revisit or residual scale. We open-source LoopTitan and release 17 pretrained models (including LoopTitan-Base and the control). Our experiment record is public as GitHub issues, with predictions pre-registered and the full exploration history kept. This is our Phase 1 technical report, laying the foundation for follow-up studies.

items.title: Towards Empirical Evidence of Safety Advancements that Aren't Capabilities Advancements
items.content: Recently, many AI company employees have said they want to slow the rate of frontier AI development, or pace the frontier. A recent policy proposal on how to achieve this is to limit the amount of compute which can be spent on ‘Capabilities R&D.’In order to be able to limit the amount of compute which is spent on capabilities activities, there must be a good definition of capabilities activities. I like this one by Alek Westover and Nathan Sheffield. While their definition rests on theoretical grounds, there should also be ways to provide empirical evidence of how related safety measures are to capabilities.If capabilities measures are positively correlated with safety measures, then labs could invest in their capabilities, but point at the resulting increase in scores on safety benchmarks to justify their investment to policymakers. This is called “Safetywashing” in (Ren et al., 2024), which assesses the correlations between safety measures and model capabilities, and attempt to draw a distinction between safety goals and capabilities advancements. There may be other problems with a positive correlation between safety measures and capabilities:Training models to improve on safety tests could also improve their non-safety capabilities. Some other factor could have a positive effect on both capabilities and safety measures, causing this correlation.Because of these problems with safety measures related to capability benchmarks, a desirable property for a safety benchmark to have is orthogonality to model capabilities. Policymakers can then know which safety measures are correlated with capabilities, and disallow R&D compute for those measures. (Ren et al., 2024) provides some empirical evidence on the relationship between capabilities and safety measures. However, that paper was published in 2024, and capabilities have advanced a lot in the past two years. In this post, I test the correlation between safety measures and model capabilities using data on safety...

items.title: Model Personas Are Not Language Agnostic
items.content: There has been much work over the past year about the persona selection model (PSM) as a plausible explanation for huggingface cybersecurity incident. I would like to extend this line of reasoning to a build a mechanistically backed explanation for the ease of conducting jailbreak attempts in low resource languages. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18239 Ultimately, I show some preliminary results that, according to the Assistant Axis paper from Lu et al in low resource languages, models (Qwen 3.5 here) adhere poorly to the personas they are trained to represent in low resource languages. This finding implies that mid-training and post-training in English does not necessarily generalize to other languages and safety work must natively consider a diverse group of languages. Background:The Persona Selection Model:"We describe the persona selection model (PSM): the idea that LLMs learn to simulate diverse characters during pre-training, and post-training elicits and refines a particular such Assistant persona. Interactions with an AI assistant are then well-understood as being interactions with the Assistant—something roughly like a character in an LLM-generated story. We survey empirical behavioral, generalization, and interpretability-based evidence for PSM. PSM has consequences for AI development, such as recommending anthropomorphic reasoning about AI psychology and introduction of positive AI archetypes into training data. An important open question is how exhaustive PSM is, especially whether there might be sources of agency external to the Assistant persona, and how this might change in the future." - tldr from Marks et al "The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans"Low Resource Language Jailbreaks:"Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attempts that circumvent safety guardrails. items.title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
items.content: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

items.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
items.content: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

items.title: Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM: Benchmarking Multimodal Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Forgery Pipelines

items.title: G0.7: Scaling Up a Fast World Action Model with Long Context
items.content: G0.7 uses long visual histories, including human demonstrations, to choose robot actions without generating future video at inference. It stores observations in a sliding-window cache and supports up to five minutes of context. On the Galaxea R1 Lite, it succeeded in 54% of 50 zero-shot trials, versus 12% for a matched robot-only checkpoint, associating the gain with added human ego video.

items.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
items.content: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

Surprisingly, the resulting policy transfers to inference with the reasoning block active and recovers teacher-level performance.
items.reasoning: A counterintuitive and well-evidenced finding: CoT is dispensable for distillation even when used at inference. This has meaningful implications for distilling from closed-weight teachers that hide their reasoning.

items.title: On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation
items.content: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.

items.summary: CodecOPSD combines a classical-codec-inspired token pruning method that discards redundant spatiotemporal tokens with an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy that trains a DiT adapter to mimic the codec pruning pattern without quality loss, enabling efficient all-in-one video generation.
items.reasoning: A principled connection between classical video compression and modern token-based generative models is appealing. The on-policy distillation adapter is a practical way to bake pruning into a DiT, with clear efficiency wins for all-in-one video models.

items.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
items.content: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

items.summary: S-Mind internalizes multi-view geometry inside a multimodal LLM through a compact set of spatial tokens supervised to hold a fused 3D scene and re-emit it from any viewpoint the reasoning chain adopts. items.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
items.content: OmniAct conditions a shared policy on each arm’s camera-relative joint geometry and predicts actions for its joints. In 2,000 simulated episodes with held-out embodiments and scenes, it achieves 63.0% success across six tasks at a 500-step cap, versus 57.9% for UMI all-views. Zero-shot, it succeeds in 13 of 20 OpenYAM setups, versus 7 for a baseline; evidence covers one arm and pick-and-place.

items.summary: OmniAct trains a single robot manipulation policy that conditions on each arm's camera-relative joint geometry so it can generalize across very different embodiments. In 2,000 simulated episodes across held-out robot bodies it reaches 63% success on six tasks and improves zero-shot transfer on the OpenYAM benchmark. The work matters because embodiment-agnostic policies reduce the cost of deploying manipulation to new hardware.
items.reasoning: Solid cross-embodiment result with credible authors including Ranjay Krishna, but real-world evidence is limited to a single arm on pick-and-place tasks, keeping it below top-tier importance.

items.title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
items.content: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.

items.title: DiffGR00T: Execution-Aware Differentiable Training for Humanoid Whole-Body Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: DiffGR00T trains a humanoid vision-language-action model to account for execution errors by differentiating a learned world model through a frozen SONIC controller and its flow-matching sampler. It updates the action head using short-horizon body-state losses. In HumanoidArena simulation, average success across four tasks rises from 59.2% to 71.7%; this comparison does not establish real-world success gains or show that gradients alone caused them.

items.summary: DiffGR00T trains a humanoid vision-language-action model against a learned differentiable world model wrapping a frozen SONIC controller and its flow-matching sampler, using short-horizon body-state losses. In HumanoidArena, average success across four tasks rises from 59.2% to 71.7%. Execution-aware training is a notable humanoid control direction.
items.reasoning: Interesting differentiable-through-controller training recipe for humanoid policies, but gains are simulation-only and confounded with non-gradient factors.

items.title: Generation as Reverse Encoding
items.content: RevFlow generates images by reversing a frozen visual encoder’s hierarchy: it generates deep semantic features, uses them to guide shallow spatial features, then decodes them into pixels. A shared Transformer supports both stages. On class-conditional ImageNet 256×256, RevFlow-XL reaches 1.96 FID after five epochs; an adapted variant reaches 2.85 FID at two evaluations, under a separate setup.
items.author: Cheng Shi, Sibei Yang, Hanzhong Guo, Yipeng Qin, Pietro Lio, Yizhou Yu
items.summary: RevFlow proposes generating images by reversing a frozen visual encoder: a shared Transformer predicts deep semantic features, conditions shallow spatial features on them, and decodes to pixels. items.title: SceneDesigner++: A Unified 9-DoF Pose Control Framework for T2I and T2V Generation
items.content: Precise 9-DoF pose control is essential for visual content generation, enabling users to specify object location, size, and orientation in 3D space. However, existing methods typically focus on either text-to-image (T2I) or text-to-video (T2V) generation, with limitations in pose controllability and temporal coherence. We present SceneDesigner++, a unified framework for 9-DoF pose control across both T2I and T2V generation. We construct ObjectPose9D++, a dataset containing high-quality images and videos with accurate pose annotations. Trained on ObjectPose9D++, SceneDesigner++ combines absolute and relative pose encoding strategies to decouple frame-wise spatial grounding from inter-frame motion modeling. Specifically, absolute pose encoding leverages CNOCS map sequences to provide explicit, frame-wise 9-DoF pose guidance. Meanwhile, our relative pose encoding, termed VPRoPE, incorporates relative pose information into rotary position embeddings to explicitly model inter-frame pose transitions, thereby promoting temporally coherent object motion. A learnable orthogonal transformation is further introduced for each attention head, allowing different heads to capture complementary geometric relationships while preserving input feature norms to promote training stability. We further adopt a two-stage training strategy to learn the absolute and relative pose encoding mechanisms separately. Benefiting from this lightweight and decoupled design, SceneDesigner++ also supports integration with an independently trained camera-control module, enabling separate or joint control over object and camera motion. Finally, we introduce T2IVPoseEval, a benchmark for evaluating diverse object poses and motion patterns in both T2I and T2V tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SceneDesigner++ consistently outperforms same-backbone baselines in pose fidelity and motion quality.

items.title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
items.content: CovNovBench evaluates six frozen covariate-aware time-series foundation models zero-shot on 88,476 series, comparing forecasts when future treatment values are novel for a series with in-distribution cases. RMSSE was higher in 52 of 54 same-model, same-dataset comparisons; TimesFM-2.5 and Moirai-1.1 were exceptions on MIMIC3-Synth POLICY-SWITCH. These scenario-level results do not establish causal effects, and POLICY-ONSET lacks matched histories.

items.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
items.content: Uni-MOPD combines five multimodal specialists sharing a base model, then refines the uniform merge with short multi-teacher on-policy distillation. The student generates responses to domain-tagged queries, and the corresponding frozen teacher supervises them. Across 19 benchmarks, the merge scores 67.6 before training and 69.8 after 50 updates, within experiments on one model family.

items.title: Operationalizing a pre-training R&D pause
items.content: OpenAI’s Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki recently said:“I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it.” [emphasis mine].Inspired by Jakub’s request, I propose an industry standard for pacing the frontier: halt pre-training R&D for 4 months. More specifically:Limit on development: No stronger pre-trains, or algorithmic and data improvements that could lead to stronger pre-trains in the future if used.Key metric: Compute spent on pre-training R&D (defined in the appendix), verified by a third-party auditor; to enforce our development limit, we’d limit this compute spend to 0. For added assurance, we should also ensure that no lower perplexity models are trained, and generally we should ensure that there are no large-scale (10^24 FLOP or more) pre-training runs.What we’d need to achieve before going beyond the limit: Wait 4 months, and then decide whether pre-training R&D is now a good idea.DiscussionWhy not just cap perplexity? There are obvious ways to game it, such as “build a model that doesn’t use the letter Z, and thus has infinite perplexity”. items.title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
items.content: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

This explicit programmatic planning step is then rendered into the final image.
items.reasoning: A creative synthesis of 3D scene programs, coding agents, and reference-based generation that makes compositional intent explicit and inspectable. The agentic Blender-loop design is novel for this task.

items.title: Counterfactual Debugging the World Model Transfer Gap
items.content: The authors attribute real-world return gaps to consequential world-model transition errors. They replay trajectories with selected transitions replaced by world-model predictions, then use recursive, coarse-to-fine counterfactual Shapley attribution to focus computation on steps with non-negligible effects. In a planted MiniGrid test, the method recovered all causal steps through one million steps; this result depends on sparse causal errors and conditions.

items.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
items.content: InstructTTS-OPD trains a text-to-speech student to follow expressive instructions while preserving intelligibility and quality. items.title: Loop4D: Embodied World Modeling with 4D VAEs and Looped Diffusion Transformers
items.content: Predicting the outcomes of robotic manipulation requires modeling both visual appearance and evolving 3D geometry. This poses two challenges: video compression can obscure fine-grained robot motion, while jointly predicting RGB and geometry demands sufficient generative capacity. We introduce Loop4D, a framework that addresses these challenges through motion-preserving 4D representations and recurrent generative refinement. Our 4D VAE encodes RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion details and geometric structure. Our RGB VAE combines geometry-guided supervision with predictive reconstruction to reduce compression-induced motion artifacts. Our geometry VAE uses lightweight adapters to adapt pretrained RGB representations while preserving their priors. Building on these representations, our Dual-Stream Looped Diffusion Transformer maintains separate appearance and geometry streams with shared Transformer weights and cross-modal connections. By reusing Transformer blocks across loops, we increase effective depth without replicating backbone parameters, enabling models with fewer parameters to improve joint RGB-geometry prediction through additional computation. Experiments demonstrate high-quality 4D generation and validate Loop4D in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.
items.author: Gen Li, Fan Luo, Mengjun Lin, Shu Han, Bohan Li, Hao Zhao
items.summary: Loop4D is a framework for predicting robotic manipulation outcomes that combines motion-preserving 4D representations with recurrent generative refinement. items.content_html: Predicting the outcomes of robotic manipulation requires modeling both visual appearance and evolving 3D geometry. This poses two challenges: video compression can obscure fine-grained robot motion, while jointly predicting RGB and geometry demands sufficient generative capacity. We introduce Loop4D, a framework that addresses these challenges through motion-preserving 4D representations and recurrent generative refinement. Our 4D VAE encodes RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion details and geometric structure. Our RGB VAE combines geometry-guided supervision with predictive reconstruction to reduce compression-induced motion artifacts. Our geometry VAE uses lightweight adapters to adapt pretrained RGB representations while preserving their priors. Building on these representations, our Dual-Stream Looped Diffusion Transformer maintains separate appearance and geometry streams with shared Transformer weights and cross-modal connections. By reusing Transformer blocks across loops, we increase effective depth without replicating backbone parameters, enabling models with fewer parameters to improve joint RGB-geometry prediction through additional computation. Experiments demonstrate high-quality 4D generation and validate Loop4D in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

items.title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
items.content: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.

items.title: VenusOCR2.0: Towards Efficient and Effective Document Parsing
items.content: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight (sim67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.

items.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
items.content: EgoUseBench introduces a benchmark for testing whether agents can connect first-person observations and user requests to website actions. It compares six models across Computer-Use, Offline Ego Use, and Online Ego Use settings using tasks and final-state success. Mean success rates are 86.1%, 64.2%, and 63.4%, respectively; these results show a gap between tested settings, not that evolving context alone causes it.

items.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
items.content: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.

items.title: WebVibe: Multimodal Interactive Website Generation via Reverse Synthesis and Visual Self-Distillation
items.content: WebVibe and Interactive-SDPO train models for interactive multi-page website generation. WebVibe builds sites, verifies navigation and widget behavior in a browser, then derives training descriptions from passing sites. On Vision2Web L2, InteractiveCoder-9B reaches 55.15 FS versus 20.20 for its base; controlled ablations support the combined recipe, not either component alone.

items.title: MaskedVGGT: Masked Multi-View Transformers Are Scalable 3D Learners
items.content: Multi-view feed-forward models show strong scalability, but their reliance on costly geometric annotations limits data scaling. Existing 3D self-supervised approaches reduce this reliance through cross-view completion (e.g., CroCo, MuM, Muskie) or novel-view synthesis (e.g., RayZer, E-RayZer), typically learning image representations and cross-view interactions jointly. We argue that learning single image representations from scratch is unnecessary for 3D pretraining methods, as doing so fails to benefit from the continuing advances in 2D foundation models (e.g., DINO, CLIP, frontier VLMs). We introduce MaskedVGGT, which freezes a strong pretrained 2D encoder and pretrains only an added, randomly initialized multi-view transformer, focusing on learning interactions across views. MaskedVGGT pretrains the multi-view transformer through masked self-distillation without annotations: a student predicts targets at masked locations based on complete anchor views and heavily masked remaining views, while an exponential-moving-average teacher provides prediction targets based on unmasked inputs. In experiments across model sizes up to 1B parameters, MaskedVGGT pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms single-stage supervised VGGT-$\Omega$ training with the same training data, model architecture, and total number of optimization updates. MaskedVGGT also outperforms E-RayZer, CroCo, MuM, and Muskie, providing evidence for the effectiveness of building multi-view pretraining on strong 2D representations. Finally, extending pretraining with additional unlabeled videos further improves generalization, and the learned representations transfer to diverse downstream tasks. These results demonstrate an effective division of learning: reuse strong image representations from 2D pretraining and learn cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data without relying on geometric annotations.

items.title: RFW-W: Scaling Physical Asset Universes for Generative Embodied Simulation
items.content: RFW-R prepares rigid 3D assets with estimated physical properties and collision geometry, then supports task-conditioned scene composition and simulation-based policy training. In five RoboTwin tasks, policies trained with 100 demonstrations per task achieved macro success rates of 71.2% in clean tests and 41.8% under randomization, versus ManiTwin’s 55.4% and 31.2%. These are simulation results, and randomized Pillbottle-Pad favors PhysX-3D.

items.title: SPiXSeg: Rethinking MLLM-based Image Segmentation as Superpixel Classification
items.content: SPiXSeg produces segmentation masks by assigning query-conditioned labels to image superpixels and directly combining selected regions, without a mask decoder or refinement. The query-independent regions are extracted once, and the model scores them in one forward pass. With LLaVA-1.5-7B, it reaches 80.5 average cIoU versus 74.9 for refined-grid Text4Seg; masks remain limited by region boundaries.

items.reasoning: A simple and effective reformulation of MLLM segmentation with a clear efficiency win (single forward pass, no mask decoder). The approach is inherently limited by superpixel boundaries, but the simplicity is appealing.

items.title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation
items.content: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

It translates review-identified state discrepancies into concrete visual asset requirements, validates them, and propagates confirmed results to maintain identity and consistency across shots.

items.title: MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems
items.content: MeterRouter builds a language-model team by sequentially choosing agents, roles, models, and communication links under a per-query budget, using each call’s output and cost to guide the next choice. In tests, at a $0.05 budget and five-agent cap, pooled accuracy is 66.72% versus MasRouter’s 66.80%, while average cost is $0.00256 versus $0.01415 per query; results do not lead on every task.

items.title: Measuring the Political Impact of the Hugging Face Incident, Coxon Media Frenzy, and Related Events
items.content: This post is made to accompany this timeline page, which collects incidents from this time period and the political responses they influenced:AI safety political advocates have long speculated that warning shots—earlier, recoverable rogue AI incidents that legibly demonstrate the potential for existential risk from future misaligned AI systems—will be especially effective for driving political progress. In July of 2026, we saw what is now generally referred to as the Hugging Face incident. We subsequently saw the disclosure of several similar rogue agent incidents, including several by third-parties, rather than by the responsible AI companies themselves. And in September, we saw one of the largest political preference cascades towards addressing AI risk yet, triggered by a Twitter thread by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon. Given their apparent unusually high impact for building the political will needed to address AI risk, I set out to investigate their political impacts in detail[1], and whether I can draw any meaningful practical takeaways for AI safety political advocates going forward.This investigation covers July 21, 2026 to November 17, 2026, plus additional background context where relevant, for politically significant (by my own judgement) results in the U.S. explicitly or inferably influenced by rogue agent incidents, Jacob Coxon’s thread, or other relevant pieces of justification used in this time period I found. The main resources I used for finding relevant political results were aipolicydaily.org, transformernews.ai, thezvi.substack.com, dconai.org, and a handful of other resources I happened to stumble across.Thanks to Joshua Peng for providing feedback as I was writing this.Politician ResponsesWhite HouseBroadly, the Trump administration has shown staunch opposition to AI regulation, generally citing concerns of strangling innovation and losing the AI race to China or denying AI risk outright. The first major exception to this came on June 1...

items.title: Progress Report: Deprioritizing eNTK for feature identification
items.content: This post contains an update on our program to use eigenanalysis of the empirical NTK (eNTK) for mechanistic interpretability, which may be of interest to people working in this space. In previous work (see paper here and distillations here and here), we found a striking alignment of eNTK eigendirections with Fourier feature directions in a model trained on modular arithmetic. This observation, along with evidence that some eNTK eigendirections appear interpretable in a 270M-parameter language model, led us to conjecture that perhaps eNTK eigenanalysis could provide a new tool to find features for mechanistic interpretability.Given the relative simplicity of the eNTK <> modular arithmetic result, we wondered if we could theoretically understand it using mean-field theory (MFT) techniques. Specifically, we hoped to test whether two phenomena observed in the modular arithmetic case study might generalize more broadly across other situations: that (1) the eNTK spectrum developed a gap after (Fourier sum) features were learned, and that (2) the eNTK eigenvectors rotated to align with said features during learning. In the course of attempting this, we distilled an earlier equilibrium mean-field analysis of a model trained to do modular arithmetic with Langevin dynamics, and performed a new dynamical mean-field analysis of a model trained on modular arithmetic with gradient flow. Both are presented below.Our main finding is that Feature learning ≠ eNTK spectral separation ≠ eNTK eigenvector rotationas a general rule, insofar as we can engineer situations where these things come apart. This gives a theoretical reason to downgrade the eNTK <> feature learning hypothesis. In a separate post, my colleague Julian Schulz will explain that rather than being used for feature identification, the eNTK may find its proper mech interp application as a data-efficient method for model steering, for which he's found some interesting preliminary results. Review of eNTK result...
