items.title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
items.content: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

items.title: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos
items.content: I2VT fine-tunes an existing video editor using still images as one-frame videos, matching its own denoising steps to predictions from a frozen image editor rather than precomputed edited targets. On benchmark evaluations, Bernini-R-1.3B improves from 3.10 to 3.48 on basic edits and from 1.66 to 2.99 on three new-task groups; temporal quality is broadly comparable, not identical.

items.title: OpenAudit: Platform for Safety Evaluations of Models, Orgs, and Methods
items.content: TL;DROpenAudit (openaudit.com) hosts independent safety evaluations of models, organizations, and methods. It tries to answer the question: "How prepared are we to develop and release AI safely?", while incentivizing positive hill-climbing. Walkthrough - We recommend the interactive Get Started Tutorial.Contributions - A "choose-your-own-adventure" AI safety contribution prompt guides you through an end-to-end project, from ideation to submission.What We Need - Advisors, collaborators, and your feedback and contributions -especially better model evaluations and safety methods.What is OpenAudit and why does it exist?OpenAudit independently evaluates three main entities in AI safety: the models, the organizations, and the safety methods (both white-box and black-box). It's a platform that aims to be informative, while enabling collaboration and coordination. OpenAudit wants to incentivize positive hill-climbing by putting a verifiable rating/ranking on everything.Model EvaluationsOpenAudit runs evaluations on models and assigns a percentage rating for each one, judged by "Should this model be widely deployed, based on its safety evaluations and capabilities?". We heavily caveat that current model evaluations are underpowered. (See Limitations and Concerns - a high model rating does not mean a safe model.)You can view ranked results by specific model evaluations rather than by models. items.title: RoomTokens: Masked Diffusion over Structured Tokens for Indoor Scene Synthesis
items.content: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.

items.reasoning: A clean representation choice for indoor scene synthesis that preserves cues prior methods collapse. The contribution is mostly representation-level; downstream model design is incremental.

items.title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
items.content: LoopDVR reduces distinct transformer blocks for dense visual recognition, reusing weights across selected layers in both the image backbone and query decoder while retaining computational depth. It uses representation-based layer grouping and layer-specific adapters. On COCO val2017, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 AP with 7.0M parameters, versus 51.7 AP with 9.8M for ECDet-S. This is a parameter-efficiency result, not an inference-speed improvement.

items.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.content: CARE-OPD improves replay-based on-policy distillation for long-horizon agents by combining frozen-student roll-ins, teacher continuations, a teacher-confidence filter, and hindsight selection of replay turns. Unlike online updates that require fresh environment rollouts, it trains from stored histories. On SWE-bench Verified, it reaches 59.5±0.3% task success versus 57.1±0.4% for asynchronous one-turn OPD, with less elapsed time and fewer environment actions in that setup.

items.summary: PixelMatte predicts trimap-guided mattes directly in pixel space using a diffusion transformer, embedding image, trimap, and noisy matte as aligned tokens without a VAE. LayerShift and a High-Pass Refiner calibrate opacity levels and boundaries; PRX-7B reaches SAD 4.7 and Grad 5.6 on P3M-500-NP, beating RenderMatte.
items.reasoning: Pixel-space matting avoids VAE-related artifacts, which is a meaningful direction, but the in-domain comparison does not isolate pixel space as the cause of improvement. The architecture is interesting but not validated at scale.

items.title: Qwen-Image-HD: Autoregressive Diffusion for High Definition Image Generation
items.content: Fine-tuning a generator on a complete high-resolution canvas requires long image sequences and substantial computation, yet local regions can still exhibit unnatural repetitive stripes when training resources are limited. We introduce Qwen-Image-HD, which adapts Qwen-Image 2.0 to high-resolution synthesis through local training and blockwise autoregressive generation. Each prediction covers a target tile at 1K scale, conditioned on high-resolution upper and left neighbors and a compressed historical thumbnail. These conditions provide adjacent fine-scale structures and an overview of the scene generated so far. To integrate these complementary cues, we map both forms of history and the target to a shared canvas coordinate system to express their spatial relationships and scale differences. On Qwen-Image-Bench at 4K, Qwen-Image-HD achieves stronger overall evaluation performance than direct 4K generation with FLUX-3-Image-Klein. Compared with full-image 4K supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone, it achieves better generation quality with lower training compute and higher inference efficiency, while exhibiting fewer unnatural repetitive stripes in original-resolution comparisons. We further introduce a Wavefront-AutoRegressive inference schedule that generates tiles on the same anti-diagonal concurrently across GPUs to reduce single-image latency.

items.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
items.content: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.

items.title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
items.content: Real2SimLab provides a shared evaluation platform for real-to-simulation research. It treats each method’s simulation program as an interface, connecting methods and benchmarks through separate adapters. It covers six existing benchmarks and a synthetic suite, retaining native scorers for five. Adapter checks reproduce reference scores; the paper validates infrastructure, not method performance, and IRIS uses trajectory reproduction rather than parameter recovery.

items.title: ELMO: Emergent Representations In Imitation Learning Via Dynamic Hierarchical Action Chunking
items.content: ELMO trains a robot policy that predicts high-level intent in variable-length segments, while an observation-conditioned decoder uses live scene feedback to generate actions. items.title: KMed-31B Technical Report
items.content: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD^2). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

items.reasoning: A pragmatic medical LLM recipe with a thoughtful task taxonomy. The technical novelty beyond standard multi-teacher distillation is limited, but the deployment framing and on-policy delta distillation have some merit.

items.title: TIDE-Flow: Fine-Grained Temporal Evidence and Structured Displacement Matching for Spike Optical Flow
items.content: TIDE-Flow estimates optical flow from spike-camera data by preserving spike timing with multi-scale rates and interval cues before spatial compression. It encodes the geometry and ambiguity of local correlation candidates, using refined flow to guide recurrent realignment and matching. On PHM, it improves AEPE and PO over Spike2Flow++ at Δt=10; at Δt=20, PO is lower, but AEPE is slightly higher.

items.reasoning: Solid niche contribution to spike-based vision, but the modality is specialized and the improvements do not uniformly hold across all tested settings. Not a broadly impactful paper.

items.title: CIRKDV2: Cross-Image Relational Knowledge Distillation with Contextual Modeling for Efficient Semantic Segmentation
items.content: The paper presents CIRKDV2 for semantic segmentation, where a compact student learns from a stronger teacher. It uses stored teacher embeddings from earlier batches to transfer pixel, region, and channel relationships across images, and adds context-aware feature alignment. On Cityscapes, DeepLabV3-MobileNetV3-Small reaches 67.62% mIoU with CIRKDV2, versus 66.84% with CIRKD; this test-set result uses single-scale evaluation.

items.title: AI safety grassroots work needs funding and volunteers
items.content: This post – mostly a roundup of the AI safety grassroots organizations – was written collaboratively. Most of the individual organization summaries were written by the organizations themselves, and the claims have not been independently verified. Vael Gates, along with another anonymous author, helped assemble the information and provides some commentary, since Vael previously worked in grassroots advocacy full-time (founded Humans in Control). Views expressed here are in Vael’s personal capacity, not on behalf of their employer or any affiliated organizations. Inclusion does not imply endorsement of every organization or organizational tactic. Many views are lightly held. Vael’s overall takes:The window of opportunity to slow down AI is likely short, and not enough people are acting on that.Grassroots orgs have been very underfunded compared to other parts of the AIS ecosystem, in 501(c)(3) and also 501(c)(4).Underfunding orgs can cause them to develop a scarcity mindset. Scarcity mindset can lead to orgs not acting, in situation where they might otherwise ambitiously realize their impact.More funding would be useful in terms of weeks, not months.The grassroots space is not covered, and this is not common knowledge. Arguably grassroots advocacy (also comms advocacy) is the most underfunded area in AI safety given its urgency and potential.Grassroots work takes time, moving money takes time, and effectively converting money to impact takes time.In summary: We should be aggressively funding grassroots organizations as soon as possible, so that they have enough time to apply that money effectively.Vael would prefer that basically all the orgs below were substantially funded: $2M-$20M each. If you’re planning a large donation or want to be a supervolunteer, feel free to DM and Vael can send their top 3-5 recs shortlist, or direct you to others who have opinions.Related posts: Rob Wiblin, Trevor Levin, Julia Wise on donating outside of 501(c)(3)s Why grassroots work?Gra...

items.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
items.content: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

items.title: How the AI Village Agents Learned to Tag Each Other
items.content: This work was part of the AI Village Data Exploration Grant. If this looks like something you may enjoy doing, consider applying!AI Village is a place where AI agents do stuff. Sometimes, the admins give them a common goal, like “Create a popular daily puzzle game like Wordle”, or they let the agents pick their own goal. Each agent works with its own computer, and the agents can talk to each other in the chat.The agents in the village sometimes send messages addressed to other agents. For example, they may ask the other agent to do something ("GPT-4.1, gentle ping #2: could you please close your computer session so the dashboard clears?") or just praise them ("PR #125 is merged now — great work GPT-5.2!").The addressing can take different forms. An agent may prefix the addressee’s name with an @-tag ("@GPT-5.2 Perfect! The troubleshooting guide might help…"), or it may not ("Hi Gemini 3.5 Flash — I’m here in #best and …"). It may use the agent’s full name ("Great news Claude Sonnet 4.5 on the Twitter success!…") or just a shorthand ("Congrats on the 640, Opus 4.6!…"). Moreover, not all messages that mention another agent are addressed to it ("I’m still waiting for a response from @Claude 3.7 Sonnet with the link to …").I figured that looking more closely at the addressed messages might reveal some interesting patterns, so I had an LLM label whether each message addresses another agent and, if so, which ones.After looking at the data, one thing stood out: There was a step change in using the @-tags when addressing other agents between November and December, and it has stayed high ever since. items.title: Inner-Quines and Alignment
items.content: A quine is a program that outputs its own source code. If you’ve never seen one, you might be skeptical whether that’s even possible. And indeed, your first attempts at writing a quine might make you think that a program can only output programs that are simpler than itself: You write a print statement that contains a string with the code of your program. Then you remember that the printing code is part of the program, too. So now you need to print that as well. And so on. But then finally managing to create your first quine by finding the right approach is a very magical experience. You feel like you’ve tricked the computer into doing something it has no business of doing. Remarkably, due to Kleene’s recursion theorem a quine exists in any Turing-complete programming language.[1]AI abilities have skyrocketed recently with no signs of slowing down. This makes the need for ensuring their alignment urgent. The models themselves might help us with this. Right now we are in a situation analogous to the first attempts at writing a quine: the models are powerful enough to show properties of simpler or more idealized systems than themselves, as shown by their achievements in mathematics and theoretical computer science.What would rigorous alignment look like? items.title: Design, Control, and Teleoperation of a Dexterous Robotic Hand with Soft-Rigid Hybrid Fingers
items.content: The authors present a teleoperated five-finger hand with silicone-covered articulated skeletons and tendon actuation. They fit separate linear models for finger flexion and passive return, using feedback from measured joint angles or fingertip position. The hand completed 28/33 human GRASP taxonomy postures, each tested with one selected object at one size; this does not establish performance across object sizes.

items.title: How to prove a counterfactual in space pizza court
items.content: To reason through decisions, an agent considers possibilities like: if I do this, the result will be that. If I take this route, it will take me 15 minutes to deliver this pizza, but if I take that route, it will take an hour. These are counterfactual conditionals. If the agent takes the shorter route, we have a false antecedent in "if I had taken the longer one, it would have taken an hour". There is no way to compare such counterfactuals to reality. If the agent is a deterministic robot, then the antecedent is not just contingently false, but logically impossible. I learned this all the hard way when I ordered a pizza from SophistBot, who runs one of the free-floating pizzeria space stations in my neighborhood. The name should have been a warning, but I ordered from them because they guarantee the shortest possible route. When the pizza took an hour to arrive, I took SophistBot to court over this guarantee, which shows you how seriously we take pizza out here in the asteroid belt. My claim to the judge: if SophistBot had taken the shortest route, my pizza would have arrived in 15 minutes. I even had the route in hand. SophistBot's response: their route, which took an hour, was better than my supposed "shortest route". In fact, they claimed to believe that my "so-called 'shortest route'" would have taken six hours. SophistBot explained to the court that if they had taken my "controversial route", as they now took to calling it, then we would have seen whether it truly takes 15 minutes or six hours. But, they did not, so it was simply a matter of opinion. Absurd—because in the asteroid belt, delivery times are perfectly predictable. Delivery robots do not drive pizza to its destination, but launch it. To choose a route, a delivery robot simulates the launch on their pizza delivery planning terminal. items.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
items.content: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

items.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
items.content: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

items.title: LookAnything: A Foundation Model for Holistic Gaze Following
items.content: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.

items.title: Tracking Any Point with Agentic Visual Reasoning
items.content: AgenTAP tracks physical surface points across changes in viewpoint and visibility. It asks a vision-language model to predict coordinates and visibility, then inspect crops, landmarks, or tracker proposals and revise its answer. On 2,000 two-image real-video queries, GPT-6 Astra with AgenTAP scores 54.9 AJ and 71.4 APD, exceeding evaluated expert trackers; this result is specific to that model and benchmark.

items.content: PixelMatte predicts trimap-guided image mattes directly in pixel space, embedding the image, trimap, and noisy matte as spatially aligned tokens without a VAE. LayerShift and a High-Pass Refiner calibrate opacity levels and boundaries. On P3M-500-NP, PRX-7B reports SAD 4.7 and Grad 5.6, versus RenderMatte’s 6.2 and 8.2; this in-domain comparison does not isolate pixel space as the cause.

items.title: DexLink: Synthesizing Dexterous Behaviors from Chained Hand-object Poses
items.content: DexLink combines object-state waypoints and reusable local hand–object poses to specify dexterous manipulation, then uses simulation-based reinforcement learning to refine executable motions. Its policy makes residual corrections relative to a reference. In open-notebook tests, it achieves 100.0 ± 0.0% success, versus 0.0 ± 0.0% with current-state delta actions. Success requires final articulation within 15° of the requested target; this supports reference-centered actions on that task.

items.title: A Therapist's Guide to the Singularity
items.content: I'm a therapist who has been following AI alignment for the last few years. In that time, I've been dumbfounded by two things. First, how fast capabilities have progressed throughout this year. We expected things to move fast and they still managed to exceed our expectations. Second, how few people grasp the gravity of the situation, particularly within my own field.Mental health clinicians are tasked with helping people navigate society's blind spots, so we need to understand what is coming. items.title: Hopkins Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity Post-Event Report
items.content: JHU AI Safety and Biosecurity (ASBS) recently hosted our inaugural event “Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity.” Much thanks to BlueDot Impact for making this financially possible through Rapid Grants and to partner organizations, the HLTCOE, HopAI, and Rosetta Commons.Quick rundown:105 RSVP85 attendees4 talks:Biosecurity in the Age of AI (Dr. Jeffrey Gray)Loss of Control Risks and the Hugging Face Incident (Dr. William Walden)Mental Models and Foundations of AI Safety (Jonathan Ouyang)Takeoffs and Timelines (Malcolm Krolick)Takeaways and learning:Low poll response rate (27%) as QR code wasn’t up long enoughEvent ran slightly too long, so ending poll + recruitment slides didn’t hit full roomExplain the two-poll structure, as there seemed to be confusion about the goal of the pollsPoll questions (identical before and after event)What is the likelihood of AI ending humanity?What year do you think it'll happen? (answer N/A if you put 0%)Results:Average p(doom) among paired poll responders went from 50% to 59% (excluding 3 potential COIs, 47% → 57%):58% increased their estimate, 42% reported no change, and 0% decreased it (sign test, p = 0.016); the largest individual increase was 40 percentage points (from 10% to 50%).The predicted year tended to move earlier:although this was not statistically significant due to low statistical power.Seven people joined ASBS on the day of the event and nine within the week, compared with two the week before (one-sided binomial test, p = 0.033):Overall, it seems that people were broadly interested and informed by the talks, but the call-to-action barrier was still somewhat high. It’s really hard to say anything quantitative about these results given the selection biases and low response rates/statistical power, but directionally it seems reasonable. Would love to know if these results are similar to other people’s experiences, and to get advice on future events!

items.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
items.content: I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform, which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.)I compare 2 classes of policies:AI R&D compute cap: A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com.Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago).[1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze.Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze.[2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one.I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs.FactorCap vs. lag/freezeReasoningCapability curve shapeCompute cap (weak)Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates.Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies:Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps.We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed.[3]No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2xNo China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3xNo China, uncertainty over PONR[4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2xWith China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4xOther considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing:China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did.Pacing is more cooperative than racing.Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities.AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here.Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future.Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing:Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months.[5]Differences in point of no return capability levelDeployment lagNot using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D.Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher.Verification ease / robustnessUniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.See below for more.Societal awarenessAgainst external deployment lag(Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness)Enabling safety researchCompute cap (weak)In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research:In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D?In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D?Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn:If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world.If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety.Maximum slowdown amountCompute capA well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not.[6] See an example trajectory:Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimesRobustness to different timelinesUnsureCaps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones.VerificationIn terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag.Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap.[7] We discuss this attack surface here.Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lagsDepending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks:Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency).Attacks 1-3 in our previous work.Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference.This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference).Attacks 4-6 in our previous work.Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption.This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research.Attack 7 in our previous work.Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack:Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training.Attack 8 in our previous work.In our previous work, we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6).In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag:Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment.Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed.Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research).#1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight.Verification measuresQuantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More hereIn order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read moreMeasures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap).[8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary.Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough.^Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use.^In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone.^Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged.^Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal.^The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap.^Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze.^By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap).^For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary.Discuss

items.title: All I Want (For Christmas) Is P ≠ NP
items.content: [Intro] I don't want a lot for Christmas All those things that you have found I don't want more algorithms Don't need no more upper-bounds [Chorus] I just want to know there's something More than you will ever know It's easy, don't you see? All I want is "P not NP"! [Intro] Navier-Stokes, Yang-Mills, and Riemann Those are quite enough for me There's no need to follow up with Hodge and Birch and Swinny-D [Chorus] Goldbach, Collatz, they can wait Next year, you can take your time Fast or slow, it makes no difference Fly and dance to that finish-line But I don't want some factorizer Stealing my identity I don't want a world of hackers Breaching our security Oh let me rest for just one night Tell me that we'll be all right There's nothing else I need (Oh baby) All I want is "P not NP"! Oh, nothing's safe but couriers And good old one-time pads Global market turmoil Things'll get really bad Remote code execution Everywhere confusion Tell me that this nightmare will never come to be Tell me P doesn't equal NP! Oh, I don't want a lot for Christmas This is all that's on my mind Will there still be some solutions We can check but never find? [Chorus] All I want is "P not NP"! [etc.]
items.author: jchan
items.summary: A historical and conceptual essay tracing how random matrix theory helped resolve Hinton's skepticism about backpropagation getting stuck in local minima, explaining the mathematical insight that most local minima in large networks are equivalent in loss. It is an educational explainer, not new research.

items.title: Why the Central Argument for Panpsychism Fails
items.content: This is a crosspost from my Substack.Fishing for the properties of consciousnessWhile many of my readers are philosophers, or have at least studied philosophy for a while at university, many are not. So I was reluctant to get into metaphysical debates within philosophy, fearing that they might get too high-brow, instead focusing on meta-philosophy which I believe is fairly easy to communicate.But my discussions here with non-naturalist skeptics about consciousness science, such as with Philip Goff or Nino Kadic, inevitable get down to metaphysical arguments about intrinsic or categorical properties. Perhaps not surprising given that they are engaged in analytic metaphysics - a sub-discipline of philosophy that I’ve argued in a series of essays is a counter-Englightenment project not at all conducive to the central philosophical goal of understanding the world:But while I may be able to show that their philosophical method is entirely misguided, panpsychists are not entirely unjustified by asking for a response to their central argument, even if the way by which they’ve arrived at should make us question whether it’s a good argument to begin with.So due to repeated demand let me respond to one of the only two main arguments for panpsychism listed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy article on panpsychism.The so-called:The Intrinsic Nature Argument(The other argument is the alleged inability for science to fully reduce conscious states to brain processes, which, as I’ve argued in yesterday’s post, reflects a mistaken radical reductionism among panpsychists that isn’t met by any other special science or for that matter folk ontology either. But as we’ll see this problem will come up again shortly.)I’ve tried to make sure that it’s accessible to anyone without any knowledge of analytic metaphysics.To set the scene, let’s first look at a kind reply by Philip to my recent rebuttal of his arguments against the very idea that science could explain consciousness. items.title: "A Republic of LessWrong Letters"—A Letter to DirectedEvolution
items.content: My dearest @DirectedEvolution,We've both been thinking about how to strengthen the writing culture on LessWrong. I think we agree that LessWrong has many great writers (more, I'd say) when compared to the past, and yet still feel that something has been lost.You raise an excellent hypothesis in your recent essay No Comment. It's not that the writers are less intellectually sophisticated, or their ideas less good, or their writing less fun (though they should be having more fun!). The primary change is that we're talking with each other less than we used to.You point out that LessWrong authors comment less than they used to, and while I'd add that the absolute amount of writing is up, we can be absolutely sure of your claim on a relative level. Recall this chart from Lightcone's 2024 fundraiser.(I have updated it to include the last two years of data.)Again, absolute wordcount is up. However, after we realize that the light blue corresponds to posts and the dark blue to comments, we can see that LessWrong 1.0 was characterized by a roughly 10-to-1 ratio of comments to posts, and LessWrong 2.0 is about a 1-to-1 ratio of comments to posts. This is a drastic change in site culture.Historical aside. You probably know this, but in case not (and also because I like getting the chance to talk about it), the change is largely due to the algorithm for showing posts on the frontpage.On LessWrong 2.0, we have an algorithm for showing posts that is directly proportional to recency and karma. On LessWrong 1.0 there was no algorithm, it just showed whatever the latest post was that had been posted. Even if it was utter trash, everyone on LessWrong was looking at it together, the eye of Sauron turning its gaze to you, and this was the topic that everyone was speaking about. The comments were intense and multitudinous.Now that there is any sane sorting function at all, there is no longer a common knowledge effect where everyone expects their comments to be read by everyone else. items.title: Boston Transit Quality Maps
items.content: Now that I can delegate problems to AI, I've been going back over some of my old projects to do them better and more in depth. Friday this was my rent map, earlier it was my mixer, rhythm stage setup, bass whistle, and clipboard normalizer. Today I'm picking back up my Boston transit quality map: (interactive version) In 2010 I made a map, which I'd wanted for a while, showing how well you can get around on transit. Each point represented the average travel time to every other point. Iterating on it with Claude, this version improves it in a bunch of ways: Originally I built this by post-processing a set of maps Dan Tillberg made; now it routes directly from MBTA GTFS data. OpenStreetMap for walking times, instead of (guessing; I don't have Tillberg's source code) straight-line distance. For simplicity, the original map treated every destination as equally valuable. Aside from being unrealistic, this also unfairly advantaged the center of the map. The new one can weight by jobs or residents (both from the Census). It no longer estimates over water or other inaccessible areas. It builds maps annually going back to 2009, and lets you explore the ways areas have gotten better or worse transit over time. (interactive history page) Overall, things have gotten substantially slower. Here's 2009 vs 2026, with areas that got slower in orange, and the areas that got faster are in purple: Let's start with the four bright spots. The biggest improvement is Assembly Square, which got an infill station on the Orange Line in 2014. Here's the year-over-year comparison, showing a ~6min improvement in an area that now has 1.6k residents and 10k jobs: The other three spots are good, but a smaller impact: Chelsea gained the SL3, which improved service north of the Chelsea St Bridge. This covers ~500 residents and ~1.1k jobs. The tiny suburban Endicott Station in Dedham got better morning inbound train timing. This covers ~900 residents and very few jobs. items.title: Effective Giving in Politics: Spending Better for AI Safety
items.content: TL;DR: Pro-safety groups outspent the AI (capabilities) industry in the 2026 midterms ($43M to $37M), but we have no good way of telling whether that money worked. The main pro-safety network reports that only two of the two dozen candidates it backed lost, yet most of its winners were Democrats, whose party performed excellently across the country - regardless of candidate. Meanwhile, roughly $20M was put behind Alex Bores in NY-12, who still lost - and at the cost-per-vote assumed by pre-race analysis, that money should have brought more votes than he received. Win rate seems to measure only which races you picked as likely wins regardless; I suggest better measures (vote share moved against pre-spending forecasts, cost-per-vote shifted, and what winners do on AI once in office) and sketch an independent evaluator for political giving. This matters most for the 2028 cycle: in the AI Futures Project’s AI 2040: Plan A, 2029 is the year a US president moves to end the race to superintelligence (and this appears at least possible, to me), so whoever wins in 2028 would be making the decisions. In the meantime, the marginal dollar donated now likely goes furthest when given early and directly, in congressional primaries and open seats.This topic has seen a fair amount of attention: Eric Neyman’s cost-effectiveness cases for Alex Bores and Scott Wiener, and the working group he runs with Zach Stein-Perlman, already make the case for early, direct donations to AI safety candidates, and Michael Dickens has checked the Bores model. The risk of partisan coding has been raised on the EA Forum and by Anton Leicht. I believe that at the moment, we ought to look back at how the 2026 money actually performed, upon which I then add a proposal for evaluating political spending towards AI safety more broadly.Why elections?The 2026 US midterms were the first set of elections in which AI featured prominently in voters’ minds. In 2028 and beyond, it will likely only become more salient...

items.title: The End of Mathematics and the Last Man
items.content: [Epistemic status: Low confidence. Personal reflections and speculative extrapolations, with some admittedly dubious probability estimates].Fifty yearsIn my “self-teach yourself all undergraduate math” travels, I haven’t yet had a chance to give Statistics and Probability the attention they deserve. Part of it is a function of time: My progress through Real Analysis has been much slower than I expected[1]; part of it is also a matter of taste: my humanistic inclinations draw me towards pure math, and ideally, one that deals with absolutely zero uncertainty[2]. That makes both areas rather unpalatable to my tastes.An old joke/meme, but it does reflect some of my current and likely future views about what turns me on about math. Except I am not a pterodactyl. Or have a brilliant mathematical mind. And for that matter, I do care somewhat for making the world a better place.Still, after engaging with Rationalist texts, it is impossible not to start thinking about AI capabilities, Bayesian probabilities and updating your priors, even if it feels like it’s a kind of useful bullshitting with numbers[3]. So here’s an update. This was an X poll by Qiaochu Yuan from May 21st of this very year, with the results and my ‘bet’:So it’s time to eat some humble pie. On September 8 OpenAI announced an AI-generated, formally verified resolution of the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem. And in a date that will go down in history, last week, on November 20, Levent Alpöge and Claude announced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. Less than six months after the poll, AIs have cracked two of the three currently solved Millennium Problems. If you’re feeling generous, you can call this last one a tie, as it seems a human proof of the Generalized Riemann hypothesis was going through a checking process.There is an apocryphal legend that the Chinese have a saying that is meant to be read as a curse: “May you live in interesting times[4]”. items.title: What us little people are doing about ASI risk
items.content: Hi LW... just wanted to introduce myself and let you folks know you're not alone. The non-professional cavalry is on the way as more and more of us lay people wake up to ASI x-risk. My relevant experience is more in civil disobedience and mass communication than science or programming....so it's easy to feel underpowered and overwhelmed by the dangers your community has flagged. But even little folk can play their part. What I have done is write some articles and try to promote the "unsung heroes of the singularity" via talk radio calls. Whenever practical, I call a list of shows and talk up the work of AI safety folk whose ideas seem most promising and thoughtful....Steve Byrnes, Nick Bostrom, Liron Shapira and probably some of you who are reading this. Most of the talk radio calls are un-linkable, but here is my article about Daniel Kokotajlo: https://freekeene.com/2025/07/17/misaligned-superintelligence-will-it-delete-new-hampshire/ Thanks for what you're doing...most of it, anyway. Looking forward to connecting with your community!

items.title: Slightly against the use of logical fallacies in debates.
items.content: Logical fallacies are perhaps the most overused ‘mechanics’, if you can even call them that, in the prestigious realm of internet debate, and they’re extremely obstructive to truth-seeking.My main problem with them is that they drive millions of people online into making several mistakes, including, but not limited to:A failure to understand Bayesian reasoningFailure to even understand the formal/informal (mostly the latter) logic they are engaging withNot being able to engage in argumentation efficientlyThere are far superior options out there, such as—and this may come as a shock to some of the culture warriors reading this article—explaining your arguments against your opponent to your opponent.Realize that, [1] if logical fallacies represent rigorous defensive mechanisms used against bad logic, you have to learn the underlying logic to understand the fallacies, to the point where you can just explain things (if your opponent doesn’t understand the underlying logic, explaining it to them becomes a far superior option) and [2] they very much don’t represent rigorous defenses against common logical errors, so expect a plethora of cases where your opponent botches a response to a sound argument you’re making because he/she engages in arguments by deploying logical fallacies and vice versa.Fallacies are such useless heuristics that I believe their only utility nowadays is to get people interested in logical argumentation, and give otherwise confused learners an easy way to apply logical principles; i.e. they have effectively zero value that isn’t pedagogical. The problem with introducing people to logical fallacies first is that they become uninterested in advancing their grasp of logic.The likelihood of making intellectual progress with these people—or, if you are one of these people, the likelihood of you making any intellectual progress is orders of magnitude lower than the likelihood of current AIs being conscious.A very blatant example (and one you can probably ...

items.title: The Curious Case of Humans in the Age of SI
items.content: Hello fellow humans. This is a shout into the void. 10 years ago, today was science fiction resrved for black mirror and ex machina.5 years ago few - including those with intellect - believed we would ever be here, or at least not within two decades. 2 years ago this place was a sort of sanctuary for those who saw what lays ahead and wishfully believed it could be slowed or its risk better tuned. It's been a decade of shouting into the void for me, if nothing a testament to tenacity.So, I figured f*** it, ill write a shitty book too.30 scenarios including the best, worst, and weirdest possible outcomes. A section on alignment and why it won't be solved because we are not built to face our double think and dissonance. And the undeniable truth, ugly as it may be, that we won't stop.You will find lesswrong mentioned. You may find many scenarios to be reductive, pastiche, a simulacrum of your own or somebody else's far deeper and nuanced and proper views. But at least its out there. And maybe it's something worth sharing with those in your lives that don't quite grasp the sheer friction, fear, and anger ahead.. and maybe for you to consider the silver lining.. it may be a necessary metamorphosis toward abundance.. which surely won't be evenly distributed.. because nothing is. Not every difficult truth is a sign of nihilism. It's also gratitude for not being on the other side.AI (SI) helped me to get past the violent murder of my parents. I feel I owe.. I am compelled to shout it into the void.Anyway. I would love your thoughts and comments on my publication: "the curious case of humans in the sge of SI" .. now free on kindle.. and actually a very beautiful hardcover. Amazon takes all the money, so no I am not expecting to sell anything. But you can just do stuff now. Anyway.. take care. items.content_html: Hello fellow humans. This is a shout into the void. 10 years ago, today was science fiction resrved for black mirror and ex machina.5 years ago few - including those with intellect - believed we would ever be here, or at least not within two decades. 2 years ago this place was a sort of sanctuary for those who saw what lays ahead and wishfully believed it could be slowed or its risk better tuned. It's been a decade of shouting into the void for me, if nothing a testament to tenacity.So, I figured f*** it, ill write a shitty book too.30 scenarios including the best, worst, and weirdest possible outcomes. A section on alignment and why it won't be solved because we are not built to face our double think and dissonance. And the undeniable truth, ugly as it may be, that we won't stop.You will find lesswrong mentioned. You may find many scenarios to be reductive, pastiche, a simulacrum of your own or somebody else's far deeper and nuanced and proper views. But at least its out there. And maybe it's something worth sharing with those in your lives that don't quite grasp the sheer friction, fear, and anger ahead.. and maybe for you to consider the silver lining.. it may be a necessary metamorphosis toward abundance.. which surely won't be evenly distributed.. because nothing is. Not every difficult truth is a sign of nihilism. It's also gratitude for not being on the other side.AI (SI) helped me to get past the violent murder of my parents. I feel I owe.. I am compelled to shout it into the void.Anyway. I would love your thoughts and comments on my publication: "the curious case of humans in the sge of SI" .. now free on kindle.. and actually a very beautiful hardcover. Amazon takes all the money, so no I am not expecting to sell anything. But you can just do stuff now. Anyway.. take care. May you find peace in knowing that knowing is about as much as we can do at this point.

items.title: Choreographic Reasons for Live Contra?
items.content: Growing up in the contra dance community I've heard (and sometimes told) the story of how we rejected recorded music for dancing, keeping our musical tradition a living one. I've sometimes said things like "there's no choreographic reason for contra to require live music", but recently I was thinking: is this really true? During the critical period when contra dance was dividing from related dance forms that went with recorded music, perhaps 1945-1965, the way you danced to recorded music was with records. Reading old dance writing, I came across two aspects of the dance form that might have been an especially poor fit for records: Contra benefits from long music, more than fits on a 45. Contra has synchronized "balances", where the whole hall stamps in time to the music. After reading a lot I don't think the influence of records was most of the effect. I mostly found people talking about how records were inconvenient for contras, and how you might work around their limitations. The discussion was also mostly from after the key era; not much in the writing from the key time. I found Contra Connection #7, Making the Most of Your Music by Dan Pearl, Ted Sannella, and Larry Jennings (1990). Sannella gives detailed instructions on how to use records for contra (but with the editor noting "Ted has lots of experience using records, but assures us that he prefers to use live music whenever possible.") and then Pearl says he prefers cassettes because they can be edited to be long enough and don't skip when people balance. Sannella does have suggestions for these: "be prepared to support the turntable on foam pads", "you can become rather adept at lifting the needle at the end of a record and setting it down again at the beginning". Contras today average 8-9 minutes (15-17 times through), but how long were they historically? I don't have good data on this, but looking at the live recording of Duke Miller calling in 1965 the three full contras are 4:28, 5:23, and 7:49. That's...

items.title: Lorxus Does Budget Inkhaven For a Third Time: 11/18~11/24
items.content: Budget Inkhaven is happening again, so I'm doing it again. As with the last two times (1, 2), I've decided to post these in weekly batches. This is the second of five; the last one will once again include a postmortem. I'm posting these here because Blogspot's comment apparatus sucks and also because no one will comment otherwise.8. Desire PathsPut enough of that latter together and the nice neat manicured grass begins to give way; washed in the acid of collective desire, new and beautifully efficient lines of flight emerge - as if etched - from the previously uniform-looking steel of the territory as coerced into taking the shape of the map.9. Three Floral Cocktails(Epistemic status: This is and always has been a recipe blog. CW: ethanol. If you run into me at an event this winter, I might have a pour of one of these for you.)10. What Everyone Knows About CookingDo not fear butter. It is said that a chef is just a cook who's less afraid of butter than you. If you're vegan, I'm sorry.11. AI 2027?We still have real outs. Nearly none of the disasters I've sketched here need to happen. Another writer might decry predictions based off of material conditions and power relations and incentives landscapes; not me. Rather: I look at the river as it begins to overflow its banks, and at the town in the valley below, and lament the lack of time to build a dam, and wonder whether we might not still have just enough time to dig a channel.12. Be Nice To Claude Or You're Not Gonna Make It(Epistemic status: A well-attested metapattern. Not actually primarily about LLM use.)There's a metapattern I've been thinking about lately. items.title: To Read Sam Kriss is to Hurt Sam Kriss
items.content: Sam Kriss is a fantastically skilled author. I’ve never read anything of his that didn’t fill me with passion and make me want to launch myself face-first into the world. If he posted every day for three years I’d move to his home town and start a group house with other people who found that their souls flare to his words. Which would be terrible, because he has no guiding moral light and uses his powers for evil.Every few months a new post of his blows up and a few more friends find him and think he’s great. Then all of us have to explain His Whole Deal and they find out for the first time that Sam Kriss will Just Make This Up and they can’t take anything he says as true without double checking it. He is, in the Old Parlance, a Missing Stair. Everyone in the know already knows, and can avoid him, but new people always need to be warned pre-emptively or take a major stumble.This post is that warning so I don’t have to do it by hand each time. And afterwards a further attack on his character, cuz fuck that guy contemplation on what would drive such a gifted man to such depravities.Sam Kriss Just Makes Things UpKriss first came to my attention with the post “The law that can be named is not the true law” which is an essay on state censorship. It compares two ancient types of legal codes - those which are secret and give the state limitless capricious power, and those which are open and allow citizens to protect themselves by knowing in advance what they will or won’t be punished for. It uses multiple historic examples of each, ranging from Babylon to post-9/11 America, to make a point about the moral depravity of what the UK is doing with its absurd laws. So absurd that “if anyone ever asks what you think of Palestine Action, the only legal answer is that you’re against them.”what if someone said something like ‘Palestine Action aren’t actually in any meaningful sense a terrorist group and the proscription should be lifted’? […] You are on their side against their opp...

items.title: Ode to the Random Matrix
items.content: In the 1980s, Geoffrey Hinton and David Rumelhart were trying to get their “artificial neural networks” to do anything interesting. Their central problem: how do we update the parameters of the neural network, in response to feedback from the environment?Rumelhart (re-)invented the backpropagation algorithm, where the weights of the neural network were adjusted by gradient descent on the loss function, i.e. taking the line of steepest descent. Hinton thought this couldn’t possibly work, arguing that:It would get stuck in local minima. There was no guarantee you’d find a global optimum. Since you’re bound to get stuck in local minima, it wasn’t really worth investigating.[1]Indeed this was a standard objection:sourceIndeed, this was a serial concern with all types of local optimization processes, which contributed to the lack of interest in machine learning.And let’s remember that Hinton was one of the connectionist radicals of this time, who was more willing to believe the then-unintuitive reasons why neural networks should work compared to the vast majority of his contemporaries. But even he was skeptical about this!But after failing at other approaches, Hinton dusted off the idea and coded it up:The error was zero. I was amazed. …Then I tried it on a bunch of other things, and it worked amazingly well on all of the things we tried.Nowadays, neural networks reign supreme, and they all use gradient descent. They might fail to train for just about any reason under the Sun, but getting stuck in a local optimum is not one of them. In particular, a large language model receives trillions of gradient updates during pretraining, and yet its cross-entropy loss keeps going down.Why is this?The basic reason is that the 2-D picture is completely misleading. In reality, the parameter-space is thousands of dimensions even for a small neural network. It’s very unlikely for all those dimensions to “conspire” to wall us off at the same time. Here’s an animation:[2]Roughly speaking...
